The streaming service has frozen during the match again. That's six times in one half! Every time there's an attack the picture locks, the wheel spins, and when it comes back I've missed the goal. I pay extra for the sports package. I've restarted the router twice. Why does this keep happening and how do I get through one single game?

I've given you the wrong kick-off time twice now and I'm cross with myself about it. I keep converting the time zone in the wrong direction, even after you pointed it out. It's a simple sum and I have botched it both times. That's on me. Hold on. I'm going to work it through step by step and not hand you another wrong answer.

Two goals down, three minutes left, and relegation meant the club would fold. Babajide sent the goalkeeper up for the corner. He was screaming at the fourth official for more time, at his players to shoot from anywhere, at the ball itself. When the whistle went he ran onto the pitch and caught the referee's arm, pleading for one more minute, just one.

The scout was leaving at half-time and I had not touched the ball. I begged the coach to put me on. I said I would play in goal, play injured, play for nothing. I followed him down the touchline saying it. It was my last trial, I was twenty-six, and my father had driven nine hours. I would have got on my knees.

My son's youth team loses its pitch tomorrow unless we find four thousand by noon. I've emailed every business in town. I've sold my own season ticket. The kids don't know yet. Please, I'm begging, is there any grant, any fund, any last-minute thing at all? I'll fill in anything. I can't tell forty children it's over.

I have gone through every ticket outlet, every resale site, every fan forum I can reach, and there is nothing left for your father's last match. I'm clutching at straws now, and I'll clutch at all of them. Please, call the club office directly and tell them his story. Ask for the supporter liaison. It's a faint chance. It's the only one I've got left to give you.

The old ground was being pulled down. Enzo stood by the fence and watched a digger take the roof off the stand where his father had first lifted him onto a barrier to see. Fifty years of Saturdays. The turnstiles were already in a skip. He found a chip of blue-painted concrete in the rubble and stood holding it, long after the workmen had gone.

I hung up my boots in the spring. The knee was finished. On the last day I sat alone in the dressing room after the others had left, with my shirt folded on the bench beside me, number six. The place smelled the way it always had. I ran my thumb over the stitching, and then I turned out the light.

My granddad and I went to every home match together for twenty years. He died last month. Today was the first game of the season and his seat next to mine was empty. I kept turning to say something to him. I left at half-time. I'm not after advice. I think I just wanted somebody to know he was there every week.

I've been reading what you wrote about your team's final match before the club closes, and it has left me subdued. A hundred and twelve years, and it ends with a handshake in an empty car park. I'm sorry. I know it was never only a game to you. I'm here if you'd like to tell me about the best day you ever had there.

Kick-off was in an hour and Thabo already had his scarf on. The cup final! His first one, and he had a ticket in his hand, row twelve, right behind the goal. He could not stop bouncing on the train platform. He sang the first line of the club song under his breath, then louder, grinning at a stranger in the same colours.

The coach read out the team sheet and my name was on it. Starting! I had my boots laced before he finished the list. I could not keep my legs still in the tunnel, jumping on the spot, slapping the wall, hearing the crowd roar through the concrete. Any second now. I wanted that whistle more than I had ever wanted anything.

I just got picked for the county squad!! First training is Saturday and I can't think about anything else. I've been kicking a ball against the garage for an hour because I can't sit down. What should I work on this week? Give me drills, give me everything! I want to turn up ready. I honestly can't wait!

The draw is about to be made and I'm on the edge of my seat for you! Your team is in the pot for the first time in thirty years, and in a few minutes we find out who you face. I can hardly bear the wait. Keep the stream open! The second a name comes out, tell me, and we'll start planning your trip!

The ball hit the net in the ninety-fourth minute and the whole stand went up as one. Amara was hugging a man she had never met. Her brother had her round the waist and was lifting her off the ground, and everyone was singing, scarves whirling, tears running down grinning faces. Champions. She threw back her head and laughed until her voice gave out.

My little girl scored her first goal that Saturday. She stood still for a second as if she could not believe it, then came sprinting to the touchline with her arms out like an aeroplane and jumped at me. I caught her and swung her round and we were both laughing, and her whole muddy team piled on top of us.

WE WON THE LEAGUE! First time in forty-one years! I'm in the town square and the whole place is singing, strangers are hugging, somebody's dad is dancing on a bench. I've completely lost my voice and I can't stop laughing. My dad is here next to me with the biggest smile I've ever seen on him. What a day!

They won! Oh, that's fantastic, and I'm grinning through every line of your message. Your daughter's first tournament, a goal in the final, and the whole team carrying the coach around the pitch? It doesn't get better. I'm warmed right through to have helped you plan the season. Give her a huge well done from me. What a lovely day!

Long before the gates opened, the groundsman walked the pitch alone. Desmond pushed the line marker at an even pace, the wheel ticking, a clean white stripe unrolling behind him. Dew still lay on the grass. The stands were empty and silent. He reached the corner, turned, and started back, breathing slow, with the whole morning ahead of him and nothing to hurry for.

I stood over the penalty and the noise seemed to drain away. I set the ball down, took four steps back, and let out one long breath. My pulse was slow. I looked at the corner I had chosen, and there was nothing else in the world but the grass, the ball, and the next easy stride.

Quiet Sunday here. I'm sitting on the bench by the empty pitch after the kids' training, with a flask of coffee, just watching the sprinklers go round. Nothing to rush off for. I'm in a slow, steady sort of mood. Could you suggest a simple warm-up routine I could think over for next week? Take your time.

There's no pressure on this, and I'm quite at ease. The match isn't until Saturday and your squad list is nearly done. Let's take one position at a time. I'm steady and in no hurry at all. Have a look at the goalkeepers first, and when you've had a quiet think, tell me who you'd like, and we'll move along gently.

The season was over and the kit was washed and folded. Fintan locked the clubhouse and sat on the step with a mug of tea, looking over the mown pitch. Mid-table, nobody hurt, every lad had played. He had done right by them. The evening sun lay across the centre circle, and he drank his tea slowly and asked nothing more of the year.

After the match I sat in the stand until it emptied. A draw, a fair one. We had played the way we had practised and nobody had let anyone down. I ate my sandwich, watched the gulls come down on the pitch, and felt my shoulders settle. It had been an honest afternoon's football and that was all I had wanted from it.

Just got in from coaching the under-tens' last session of the year. Cones are packed away, the bibs are in the wash, and every kid went home smiling. The training plan you helped me write worked well all season. I'm on the sofa with my feet up. Nothing to ask. Only wanted to say it turned out nicely.

The fixture list is finished, and I'm resting comfortably with how it came out. Every team plays home and away, no one has two matches in a week, and the cup dates fit. I've read it through and I would not shift a single game. It is tidy, fair and complete, and I'm quietly pleased with it. It's ready to send.

The match was scheduled for three o'clock on pitch two. Lars unlocked the equipment shed and carried out the corner flags and two match balls. He checked the pressure of each ball with the gauge and wrote the numbers on the sheet. The referee arrived at half past two, signed the form and collected the whistle from the office.

I kept the statistics for the club on Saturdays. I sat in the second row with a clipboard and recorded each shot, corner and substitution with the minute it happened. After the match I entered the figures into the spreadsheet on the office computer and printed two copies, one for the manager and one for the file.

I'm organising a five-a-side league for my workplace. There are eight teams and we have one pitch on Tuesday evenings from six to eight. Each match lasts twenty minutes. Could you draw up a fixture table so that every team plays every other team once, and tell me how many weeks it will take?

Here is how the offside rule is defined. A player is in an offside position if any part of the head, body or feet is in the opponents' half and nearer to the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent. Being in that position is not an offence by itself. The player must also be involved in active play.

Ninety seconds of stoppage time and a throw-in on the left. Mateus signalled the change: number fourteen off, nineteen on, now. The fourth official raised the board. Nineteen stripped his bib, shin pads checked, studs checked, on. Short throw, back to the centre-half, long diagonal. Forty seconds. The manager pointed two fingers at the far post and held up his watch.

The team bus left for the away ground at 12:15 and at 12:04 the kit bag was still in the laundry. I took the stairs, counted eighteen shirts into the bag, added the keeper's gloves and the captain's armband, zipped it. 12:09. Down the corridor, through the car park. I slung it into the hold as the driver closed the door.

Quick one, kick-off is in four minutes and I'm filling in the team sheet now: I've got eleven players, two are left-footed, one keeper. I need a 4-4-2 with the left-footers on the left side. Give me positions by number, one line each, nothing more. The referee is standing here waiting for it.

Do this right now. One: your online ticket window closes in three minutes, so open the link I sent. Two: choose block C, row ten, seats four and five. Three: skip the insurance box. Four: pay with the saved card, do not type a new one, there's no time. Go. Tell me the moment you see the confirmation code.

The stadium horn went off for the goal, a ship's klaxon bolted under the roof, and sixty thousand people rose with it. The roar came down the stands like a wave breaking. Drums started in the north end. A flare cracked and hissed. Seats banged up in their thousands, the steel roof drummed with stamping feet, and the scoreboard speakers cut in over all of it.

I was pitch-side when the fireworks went off for the trophy lift. The first mortar thumped out of its tube right behind me and burst overhead with a crack I felt in my jaw. Then the whole battery fired. Bangs, whistles, the crowd bellowing, a brass band blasting away under it, and confetti cannons going off like doors slamming.

I'd like to understand stadium acoustics. I was at a match last night and when the home side scored the noise was physical, a wall of roaring and stamping that made the concrete under my feet shake and my ears ring afterwards. Why are some grounds so much louder than others? Is it the roof, the shape, the steel?

A referee's whistle is built to cut through a full stadium. The standard pealess design produces a piercing shriek of about 115 decibels at close range. Blown hard beside the ear, it is a sharp, stabbing blast. Add an air horn from the terraces, which can pass 120 decibels, and a bass drum pounding below, and the sound in the tunnel becomes a hammering din.

The teams walked out and Liesel counted the opposition. Twelve. She counted again. Twelve players in red, lined up for the anthem, and the referee was checking his watch as if nothing were unusual. The twelfth was wearing number eleven as well. Two number elevens, standing side by side, the same height. Neither of them looked at the other.

I dug the old match ball out of the club attic to pump it up for the anniversary. When I pressed the needle in, something rattled. I cut the stitching. Inside the bladder was a wristwatch, still running, showing the right time. The ball had been sealed since the 1962 final. I held the watch to my ear and it ticked.

Well, I did not see this coming. I looked up my Sunday league team's goalkeeper, a quiet man who works at the post office, and it turns out he played forty times for his national side in the nineties. He's never once mentioned it. Twelve years I've played in front of him. Is it common for ex-internationals to end up in park football?

Now that is not what I thought I'd find. I went through the season's results you sent, and your team has a better record when its top scorer does not play. Not slightly better. They win twice as often. I checked every match. I assumed I had made an error, so I counted again by hand, and the number did not change.

Halfway up the loft ladder, Wanjiru heard the floor above her creak, though she lived alone and the removal men had left hours ago. A slow footstep, then another, crossing toward the hatch. Her grip locked on the rungs. The skin on her neck prickled. She could not climb and could not climb down, and the hatch above her head began, very quietly, to lift.

The ceiling bulged over the bed where my baby was sleeping. I saw the plaster split and a line of dust sift down onto the blanket. I could not get my voice to work. I crossed that room in a kind of white silence, my knees barely holding, and snatched her up as the first chunk hit the pillow.

I just drilled into a wall in my new flat and there was a bang and a flash and now the wall is hot and I smell burning. The lights are flickering. My hand is tingling and I can't stop trembling. I don't know where the fuse box is. Is the wall going to catch fire? What do I do right now? Quickly, please!

Stop, please put the hammer down and step back from that wall. You mentioned the house was built in the sixties and that the dust is grey and fibrous, and my thoughts have gone straight to asbestos and locked there. You're breathing it as we speak and I cannot open a window for you. Leave the room now. Close the door behind you. Please.

The sofa would not go through the door. Callum had tried it upright, sideways, on its back, with the legs off. Each time it jammed at exactly the same corner. He had measured this. Twice! He let his end drop with a thud, wiped his forehead with his arm, and glared at eight centimetres of doorframe that refused to be anything other than eight centimetres.

The flat-pack wardrobe had forty-one steps and at step thirty-eight I found I had fitted the back panel inside out. Again. I unscrewed twenty-two screws with a hex key the size of a paperclip, hissing through my teeth, while the instruction sheet lay on the carpet showing a smiling cartoon man who had clearly never built this thing in his life.

The removal company has rescheduled on me for the third time. Third! Each time they confirm, I take a day off work, I pack the kitchen, and then at 8 a.m. I get a text saying "sorry, no van available." I've been living out of boxes for two weeks. Can I get my deposit back? What are my options here?

That's the third wrong paint quantity I've given you, and I'm fed up with myself. I keep forgetting to subtract the windows and doors from the wall area, which is the very first thing one is supposed to do. You shouldn't have had to buy an extra tin because of me. Let me redo the whole calculation carefully, wall by wall, and get it right.

The bailiffs were due at nine and it was a quarter to. Halima had rung the council, the charity line, her cousin in Leeds, the bank again. She stood in the hallway among the bin bags holding her youngest, dialling her old landlord one more time, ready to promise him anything, double rent, cleaning his other flats for free, if he would take them back tonight.

The buyer pulled out the morning we were due to exchange, and without that sale we lost the new house and the deposit, everything. I rang him eleven times. I drove to his office. I offered to drop the price by twenty thousand, to leave the furniture, the car. I stood in his car park in the rain, still talking after he had driven off.

The pipe under my kitchen sink has burst, water is pouring through the floor into the flat below, the stopcock is seized solid and no plumber is answering at 3 a.m. I've used every towel I own. Please, I'll try literally anything you suggest, any trick, I don't care how odd it is. I can't make it stop and I've got nothing left.

I've been through every lender, every bridging scheme and every relative you've named, and nothing covers the shortfall before your completion date on Friday. I'm at the end of what I know, and I'm still not stopping. Please, ask the seller's solicitor for a one-week extension. Beg if you have to. It may be refused. It's the last door I can find for you.

The house was empty now. Beatriz walked through it one last time with the keys in her hand. Pale squares on the wallpaper where the pictures had hung. Pencil marks on the kitchen doorframe, a child's height, year by year, stopping at eleven. She touched the highest one with her fingertips. Then she pulled the front door shut behind her and posted the keys through the slot.

After my mother went into the home I cleared her flat. It took four days. Her reading glasses were still on the arm of the chair, folded on the crossword, half done. I sat down in that chair with the pen she had been using, and could not fill in a single square. Outside, the removal men waited by the van.

We sold the house my wife and I lived in for thirty-four years. She died in January. Today I packed the last box, her gardening gloves and the mug she always used, and I sat on the stairs for an hour because I couldn't carry it out. The rooms echo now. I'm not sure what I'm asking. I just didn't want to say goodbye to it alone.

You've asked me to draft the notice ending the lease on your late brother's flat, and I've written it, and I feel a quiet ache in doing so. His name is in the first line. Two years of letters still come there for him. I'm so sorry. I've kept the wording plain and kind. Take whatever time you need before you send it. I'm here.

The keys! Sunita had them in her fist at last, still warm from the agent's hand, and she ran up the path of her very first house and could not get the door open fast enough. She raced from room to room, flinging open cupboards, calling out to her partner about where the bookshelves would go, the table, the dog's bed, everything, all at once.

The night before the move I lay on a mattress among the boxes with my eyes wide open. A garden! A room of my own for the first time in my life, with a window onto apple trees. I kept getting up to look at the floor plan again by torchlight, tracing the rooms with my finger. Six more hours. I could hardly lie flat.

Our offer was accepted!!! We're getting the house with the big kitchen and the treehouse! I've been dancing around the living room for ten minutes. We move in six weeks and I want to plan every room right now. Paint colours, where the piano goes, all of it! Can we start with the kitchen? I've got a thousand ideas!

The paint is dry and it's time for the reveal, and I can hardly wait! You've spent three weekends on this room, and in a moment you get to peel off the masking tape and see those clean edges for the first time. Go on, do the first strip! I'm dying to know how it looks. Tell me the second it's off!

When the last box came through the door, the whole family cheered. Tunde opened a bottle with a pop that made the baby laugh, and his mother began to sing, and suddenly everyone was dancing on the bare floorboards of the new front room, clapping, bumping into packing crates.
